topics.title: Rectifiers and ripple
topics.summary: Diodes turn AC into pulsing DC; a reservoir capacitor smooths it, leaving a ripple that depends on load current, frequency, and capacitance.

lensNotes.circuit: A bridge flips both halves of the AC wave positive; a reservoir capacitor holds the peak between pulses. Ripple ≈ I/(f·C) for half-wave and half that for full-wave.
lensNotes.signals: Rectification is a strongly nonlinear operation: it creates DC plus harmonics of the line frequency. The capacitor is a low-pass filter that keeps the DC and suppresses the rest.

prerequisiteNotes.diode_models: Each conducting diode drops about 0.7 V, which is why a bridge loses about 1.4 V of the peak.
prerequisiteNotes.rc_time_constant: Ripple is the smoothing capacitor discharging into the load between peaks, at a rate set by the load and the capacitance.

goals: Find the peak output of a half-wave or bridge rectifier from the transformer's RMS voltage, subtracting one or two diode drops
Estimate the peak-to-peak ripple: ΔV ≈ I/(f·C) for half-wave and I/(2f·C) for full-wave, where f is the line frequency, because full-wave refills the capacitor twice per cycle
Predict how the ripple responds to the load current, the capacitance, and the rectifier type, and explain why a higher input voltage alone need not change it
Find the peak inverse voltage a rectifier diode must block, and explain why the diodes carry short current pulses much larger than the load current
topics.intuition: With a reservoir capacitor large enough to keep the ripple small, a rectifier's output charges to the input's peak minus the conducting diodes' drops, then sags while the capacitor alone feeds the load until the next peak refills it.
topics.why: Once the capacitor has charged to near the peak, the diodes are reverse biased for most of the cycle, conducting only while the input climbs back above the capacitor's voltage. In between, the capacitor alone supplies the load, losing charge Q = I·Δt, so its voltage falls by ΔV = Q/C. A bridge refills on both half-cycles, halving Δt and so the ripple, but its current passes through two diodes in series. All the charge the load used returns in those brief intervals, so the diode current peaks far above the load current.
topics.explanation: A transformer secondary gives a sine wave, rated by its RMS value; its peak is √2 times that. A single diode, a half-wave rectifier, passes only the positive half-cycles. A bridge of four diodes steers both halves the same way through the load (full-wave), but each half-cycle's current passes through two diodes in series. With the 0.7 V model, the output peaks at V_p − 0.7 V for half-wave and V_p − 1.4 V for a bridge. A reservoir capacitor across the output charges to that peak and feeds the load in between, sagging by the ripple: ΔV ≈ I/(f·C) for half-wave and I/(2f·C) for full-wave, where f is the line frequency (full-wave refills twice per cycle, so its ripple is at 2f). This estimate assumes the capacitor feeds the load for the whole gap between peaks, so it slightly overstates the ripple. The diodes refill the capacitor only in short pulses near each peak, so their peak current is many times the load current. When off, each diode must block the peak inverse voltage (PIV): about V_p in a bridge, but about 2V_p in a half-wave rectifier with a capacitor, whose stored voltage adds to the winding's negative peak (without the capacitor, only about V_p).

workedExample.problem: A transformer steps the 120 V RMS, 60 Hz AC line down to 9 V RMS. Its secondary feeds a bridge of four 1N4007 diodes, a 2200 µF reservoir capacitor, and a load drawing a steady 100 mA. Find the peak output, the ripple, and the average output; compare a half-wave rectifier with the same capacitor; find the reverse voltage each diode must block; and estimate the current while the capacitor recharges. Model: 0.7 V per conducting diode, an ideal transformer, and a load current that stays at 100 mA.
steps: Peak of the secondary: V_p = 9 V × √2 = 12.73 V.
Bridge (0.7 V model): each half-cycle's current passes through two conducting diodes, so the capacitor charges to 12.73 V − 2 × 0.7 V = 11.33 V.

Both half-cycles refill the capacitor, so the ripple frequency is 2 × 60 Hz = 120 Hz and the gap between refills is 1/120 Hz = 8.33 ms. ΔV ≈ I/(2f·C) = 0.1 A / (2 × 60 Hz × 2200 µF) = 0.379 V peak to peak.
The output swings between 11.33 V and about 11.33 V − 0.379 V = 10.95 V, an average of about 11.33 V − 0.379 V / 2 = 11.14 V.

Half-wave with the same capacitor (0.7 V model): one diode drop, so the peak is 12.73 V − 0.7 V = 12.03 V, but the capacitor is refilled only once per cycle, at 60 Hz: ΔV ≈ I/(f·C) = 0.1 A / (60 Hz × 2200 µF) = 0.758 V, twice the bridge's ripple.

Reverse voltage (0.7 V model). In the bridge, an off diode blocks the output plus one conducting diode's drop: 11.33 V + 0.7 V = 12.03 V, which is V_p − 0.7 V. In the half-wave circuit, the capacitor holds up to 12.03 V while the winding swings to −12.73 V, so the diode must block up to 12.03 V + 12.73 V = 24.76 V, about twice V_p. Choose diodes rated well above these, with margin.

Recharge pulses: the bridge conducts only while the rectified input, less 1.4 V, is above the capacitor, which has sagged by 0.379 V. The input must climb back to within 0.379 V of its peak: |sin θ| = 1 − 0.379 V / 12.73 V = 0.970, so θ = 76.0°. Conduction ends near the peak at 90°: about 14.0° of each 180° half-cycle, or 14.0/180 × 8.33 ms = 0.65 ms.

In those 0.65 ms the diodes must replace all the charge the load took in 8.33 ms: 100 mA × 8.33 ms = 0.833 mC. The average diode current during the pulse is about 0.833 mC / 0.65 ms = 1.3 A, about thirteen times the load current, and its peak is higher still. At these pulse currents each diode also drops more than 0.7 V, closer to 0.8–1 V, and a real transformer's winding resistance lowers and widens the pulses; both pull the peak output below 11.33 V.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Brute-Force Power Supplies", ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.3 "Diodes and rectifiers"
sources.note: The peak rectified output is √2 times the RMS input less one diode drop for a half-wave rectifier and less two drops (1.4 V) for a bridge, whose current passes through two diodes in series. An unfiltered half-wave diode blocks the full source voltage.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Brute-Force Power Supplies", ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.5 "Ripple"
sources.note: Ripple follows from I = C·dV/dt with the capacitor alone feeding the load between peaks, estimated as a sawtooth falling for half the line period (8.33 ms at 60 Hz) after full-wave rectification, which gives I/(2fC).

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Rectifier Circuits", ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.6 "Ripple"
sources.note: Ripple is quoted peak to peak, at the line frequency for half-wave and twice the line frequency for full-wave rectification.

templates.prompt: A transformer secondary gives {Vrms} RMS. It feeds a half-wave rectifier with one silicon diode (0.7 V). What is the peak output voltage?
templates.explanation: Peak of the sine: {Vrms} × √2 = {Vp}. One diode conducts, dropping 0.7 V: {Vp} − 0.7 = {answer}.
hints: Line (wall-outlet) and transformer voltages are given as RMS; convert to peak.
V_p = √2 · V_rms, then subtract one diode drop.

misconceptions.feedback: {Vrms} is the RMS value. The output charges to the peak, V_rms × √2, minus the diode drop.
Don't forget the diode's 0.7 V drop.

templates.prompt: A {Vrms} RMS transformer secondary feeds a full-wave bridge rectifier of silicon diodes. What is the peak DC output?
templates.explanation: The peak is {Vrms} × √2 = {Vp}. In a bridge, two diodes conduct in series on each half-cycle, so subtract 2 × 0.7 V: {answer}.
hints: How many diodes are in the current path at any moment in a bridge?
Two, so subtract 1.4 V from the peak.

misconceptions.feedback: In a bridge, current passes through two diodes on each half-cycle: subtract 1.4 V.

followUps.prompt: Why does a bridge lose two diode drops when a half-wave rectifier loses only one?

choices.text: Each half-cycle's current passes through two conducting diodes in series with the load
choices.feedback: Right: two diodes in the path, and series drops add (KVL), so the output peaks at V_p − 2 × 0.7 V.

choices.text: All four diodes conduct at once, in two pairs, and each pair adds its own drop
choices.feedback: Only two diodes conduct at a time. The other two are reverse biased and block; on the next half-cycle the pairs swap.

choices.text: The two blocking diodes each drop 0.7 V while they are reverse biased
choices.feedback: A reverse-biased diode carries no current, so it is not in the path to the load. The drops come from the two diodes that conduct.

choices.text: The bridge doubles the ripple frequency, and each extra pulse costs one more drop
choices.feedback: The ripple frequency doesn't set the drop. Each pulse passes through the same number of diodes: two.

followUps.explanation: Trace one half-cycle: current goes out of one end of the winding, through one diode to the load, and back through a second diode to the other end. Using the 0.7 V model from Practical diodes, the two drops add along that loop, so the peak output is V_p − 1.4 V. A bridge gives full-wave output at the cost of one extra diode drop; a center-tapped full-wave rectifier loses only one.

templates.prompt: A half-wave rectifier on {f} line power has a {C} reservoir capacitor and supplies {I} to its load. Estimate the peak-to-peak ripple.
templates.explanation: Between peaks, the capacitor alone feeds the load for about one period, 1/f. It loses ΔV = I·Δt / C = I / (f·C) = {I} / ({f} × {C}) = {answer}.
hints: The capacitor supplies the load for about one period between recharges.
ΔV = I / (f · C) for a half-wave rectifier.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the full-wave result. A half-wave rectifier recharges once per cycle, so the gap is 1/f: ΔV = I / (f·C).

followUps.prompt: Why does the ripple grow with the load current and shrink with a bigger capacitor?

choices.text: Between peaks, the capacitor alone feeds the load, losing charge I·Δt, and its voltage falls by that charge over C
choices.feedback: Right: more current drains more charge in the same gap, and a bigger capacitor loses less voltage for the same charge.

choices.text: The diode's drop grows with the load current, and a bigger capacitor pulls that drop back down again
choices.feedback: Between peaks, the diode isn't conducting at all. The droop comes from the capacitor discharging into the load, not from the diode.

choices.text: More load current charges the capacitor to a lower peak, and a bigger capacitor reaches a higher peak
choices.feedback: The peak is set by the input and the diode drop, and barely moves. The ripple is how far the voltage sags between peaks.

choices.text: The ripple is AC leaking through the diode, and a bigger load current lets more of it get through
choices.feedback: Between peaks, the diode is reverse biased and blocks. The sag comes from the capacitor feeding the load on its own.

followUps.explanation: This is the RC discharge from the RC time constant topic. The load drains the capacitor between peaks; over a short gap, the exponential is almost a straight line falling at I/C volts per second. Over one period, 1/f, that gives ΔV = I/(f·C).

templates.prompt: A full-wave bridge on {f} line power has a {C} reservoir capacitor and supplies {I}. Estimate the peak-to-peak ripple.
templates.explanation: Full-wave rectification recharges the capacitor twice per cycle, so it has to hold up only for 1/(2f): ΔV = I / (2f·C) = {I} / (2 × {f} × {C}) = {answer}.
hints: How often does a full-wave rectifier recharge the capacitor?

misconceptions.feedback: That's half-wave. A bridge recharges on both half-cycles, halving the ripple: ΔV = I / (2f·C).

steps: Between peaks, the capacitor supplies the load alone.
A full-wave rectifier recharges twice per cycle, so the gap is 1/(2f).

templates.prompt: A full-wave bridge rectifier runs from {f} line power. At what frequency is the ripple on its output?

choices.feedback: Yes: both half-cycles are flipped positive, so the output pulses twice per line cycle.
That's the half-wave ripple frequency. Full-wave fills in the missing half-cycles.

choices.text: 0 Hz, because the output is DC
choices.feedback: The average is DC, but the capacitor still discharges and recharges on every pulse.

choices.text: It depends on the load
choices.feedback: The load sets the ripple size, not its frequency.

templates.explanation: Each half-cycle of the {f} input produces a pulse, so the ripple repeats at {f2}. The faster repetition is why full-wave ripple is half as large for the same capacitor and load current.

followUps.prompt: On a scope, this bridge's ripple repeats at {f}, not {f2}, and is about twice as large as usual. What has most likely happened?

choices.text: One bridge diode has failed open, so the bridge works half-wave and refills C only once per cycle.
choices.feedback: Right: the ripple frequency counts refills; half as many refills doubles the gap and the sag.

choices.text: The reservoir capacitor has dried out.
choices.feedback: Less C makes the ripple bigger but doesn't change how often C is refilled, so it would still repeat at {f2}.

choices.text: The load current has doubled.
choices.feedback: More current deepens the sag, but the refills still come twice per cycle, at {f2}.

choices.text: The line frequency has dropped to half.
choices.feedback: The utility holds 60 Hz to a small fraction of a hertz; a halved line frequency isn't a realistic fault.

followUps.explanation: A healthy bridge refills C on both half-cycles, so its ripple repeats at {f2}. With one diode open, one half-cycle has no path to C: the circuit runs half-wave, refilling once per cycle at {f}. C now feeds the load for a whole period instead of half of one, so the sag is ΔV ≈ I/(f·C) instead of I/(2f·C), about twice as large. The other half-cycle still passes through two diodes, so the peak barely changes. Read the ripple's frequency first: it tells you how many refills there are before you think about C or the load.

templates.explanation: The capacitor charges to the input peak minus two diode drops, because the current flows through two diodes of the bridge on each half-cycle. templates.prompt: A rectifier with a reservoir capacitor feeds a load. What happens to the ripple if the load current doubles?

choices.text: It roughly doubles
choices.feedback: Right: ΔV ≈ I/(fC) (or I/(2fC) full-wave), so the ripple is proportional to the load current.

choices.text: It halves
choices.feedback: More current drains the capacitor faster between peaks, so the ripple grows.

choices.text: It stays the same, because the capacitor is the same
choices.feedback: The same capacitor loses charge faster when more current is drawn.

choices.text: It disappears, because the diodes conduct longer
choices.feedback: The diodes conduct a little longer, but the ripple still grows with current.

templates.explanation: Between peaks, the capacitor alone supplies the load: ΔV = I·Δt/C. Twice the current drains twice the charge in the same time, so the ripple roughly doubles.
hints: Between charging peaks, what supplies the load current?
templates.noDrawing: holds for any rectifier type, so no one circuit is drawn

templates.prompt: A full-wave bridge on {f} line power charges its reservoir capacitor, C = {C}, and the load draws a steady {I}. C is swapped for {new_C}. What happens to the peak-to-peak ripple?

feedback.up: A bigger capacitor doesn't discharge harder. The load still takes the same charge between peaks, Q = I·Δt, and the voltage a given charge moves is ΔV = Q/C: more capacitance holds more charge per volt.
feedback.same: The load takes the same charge between peaks, but the sag that charge causes depends on the capacitance holding it, ΔV = Q/C: a bigger capacitor stores more charge per volt.

whatIf.factorHint: The charge lost between refills, I·Δt, is unchanged, and ΔV = Q/C: look at where C sits.

templates.explanation: Between peaks, the capacitor alone feeds the load, losing charge Q = I·Δt with Δt ≈ 1/(2f). Its voltage falls by Q/C, so ten times the capacitance gives a tenth of the ripple: {before} → {after}. This is the RC discharge from the RC time constant topic: over a short gap, the exponential is nearly a straight line with slope I/C.
hints: Between charging peaks, what supplies the load, and how much voltage does it lose for a given charge?

templates.prompt: A bridge rectifier is fed from a transformer winding of {Vrms} RMS at {f}. It charges a capacitor C = {C} that feeds a load resistor R_L = {RL}. R_L is replaced by {new_RL}. What happens to the peak-to-peak ripple?

feedback.down: A smaller load resistance draws more current (I ≈ V/R_L), and between peaks only the capacitor supplies it. The charge the capacitor loses before the next peak is I·Δt, and the voltage drop that charge makes is ΔV = I·Δt/C.
feedback.same: The capacitor and the frequency are unchanged, but a smaller R_L draws more current (I ≈ V_out/R_L), and only the capacitor supplies it between peaks: the charge it loses is I·Δt, and that charge sets the sag, ΔV = I·Δt/C.

whatIf.factorHint: Ripple is I·Δt/C, and the load current is I ≈ V_out/R_L with V_out barely moving: follow R_L through both.

templates.explanation: The output sits near the peak, {Vrms} × √2 − 1.4 V = {Vo}, so the load draws about {Vo}/R_L. A tenth of the resistance draws ten times the current, and the capacitor loses ten times the charge between peaks: ripple ≈ I/(2fC) goes {before} → {after}. The peak itself barely moves; the sag between peaks is what grows. That is why supplies are specified for a maximum load current.
hints: What happens to the load current when R_L gets smaller?

templates.prompt: A half-wave rectifier on {f} line power charges a capacitor C = {C}, and the load draws a steady {I}. The single diode is replaced by a bridge; the capacitor and the load current stay the same. What happens to the peak-to-peak ripple?

feedback.up: The bridge does lose an extra 0.7 V of peak, but ripple is the sag between refills, not the height of the peak. The capacitor sags only while it alone feeds the load, ΔV = I·Δt/C, and a bridge refills it on both half-cycles, so each stretch of discharging is shorter.
feedback.same: With the same capacitor and the same current, the capacitor sags at the same rate, I/C. But a bridge refills it on both half-cycles instead of once per cycle, so the sag runs for less time before the next peak tops it up.

whatIf.factorHint: Ripple is the charge drained between refills over C, ΔV = I·Δt/C, with I and C unchanged. Work out the gap Δt for a rectifier that refills once per cycle and for one that refills on both half-cycles.

templates.explanation: Ripple is the charge drained between refills divided by C: ΔV = I·Δt/C. A half-wave rectifier refills once per cycle (Δt ≈ 1/f) and a bridge twice (Δt ≈ 1/(2f)), so the ripple halves: {before} → {after}. At the same time, the ripple frequency doubles, from {f} to {f2}.
hints: How often does each rectifier top up the capacitor?

templates.prompt: A bridge rectifier on {f} line power charges a capacitor C = {C}. A linear regulator after it draws a steady {I}, whatever its input voltage. The transformer is changed from {Vrms} RMS to {new_Vrms} RMS. Using ΔV ≈ I/(2fC), what happens to the peak-to-peak ripple on the capacitor?

feedback.up: A higher peak doesn't make the capacitor lose more charge. The regulator still draws {I}, and the sag between peaks is I·Δt/C.
feedback.down: A higher voltage doesn't make the capacitor hold up better. The sag depends only on the charge drawn between peaks and the capacitance, and neither changed.

templates.explanation: The capacitor charges to a higher peak, but between peaks it still loses Q = I·Δt with the same current {I} and the same gap, 1/(2f). ΔV = Q/C is unchanged: it stays at {before}. The whole waveform moves up; its sag stays the same. With a plain resistor load, it would differ: a higher voltage would push more current through the resistor.
hints: Which quantities set the charge the capacitor loses between peaks?

templates.prompt: A transformer steps 120 V, 60 Hz line power down to {Vrms} RMS (simulation only). Its secondary feeds a bridge of four silicon diodes, a reservoir capacitor C1, and a {RL} load. Choose C1 from the E6 series (1.0, 1.5, 2.2, 3.3, 4.7, 6.8 times a power of ten) so the ripple at the output is at most {Vr} peak to peak, but no less than half that: a larger capacitor costs more, takes more space, and draws larger charging pulses through the diodes. The simulator checks your choice with real diodes.

sim.note: The estimate I/(2fC) assumes C1 feeds the load for the whole 1/(2f). In fact the diodes start recharging it a little before each peak, and the load current falls slightly as the output sags, so the simulated ripple here is about 15–20% below the estimate.

templates.explanation: Start with the load current. C1 charges to the secondary's peak, √2 × {Vrms} = {Vp}, less two diode drops (about 0.8 V each while charging): about {Vdc}. The load therefore draws about I = {Vdc}/{RL} = {I}. A bridge refills C1 twice per cycle, so between refills C1 feeds the load alone for about 1/(2 × 60 Hz) = 8.33 ms and sags by ΔV ≈ I/(2fC). For ΔV ≤ {Vr}: C ≥ I/(2f·ΔV) = {I}/(2 × 60 Hz × {Vr}) = {Cmin}. Take the next E6 value up. The value one step below may also pass in the simulator, because the real ripple is smaller than the estimate; the next value up is the one the estimate guarantees. In the simulator the ripple comes out about 15–20% below this estimate, for two reasons: the rising half-sine meets the sagging output and starts recharging C1 before the full 8.33 ms has passed (the diodes conduct for a short stretch before each peak), and the output averages below its peak, so the load draws a little less than I. The estimate therefore errs on the safe side. The sag is close to a straight line because, for the next E6 value up, R_L·C1 is about 100 ms or more, over ten times the 8.33 ms gap: the RC discharge from the RC time constant topic, seen over a small fraction of τ.
hints: First find the load current: what DC voltage does C1 hold, and what does the load draw at that voltage?
A bridge refills C1 every 1/(2f), so ΔV ≈ I/(2fC). Solve for C and round up to the next E6 value.
